figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Measured token costs of the three disclosure tiers at tag v2.65.0, shown along a hypothetical task path. These are corpus measurements, not an agent trace. Selecting a skill uses descriptions already in standing context, so it adds no documentation tokens; Section 4 treats that step separately. The running total assumes a median skill and one median reference file. Section 5 costs the library’s documented workflows instead.
figures.headline: Resident descriptions are far smaller than instruction files and reference documents, which together make up the deferred tiers.
citing_sentences: The disclosure model has three tiers whose sizes differ by orders of magnitude (Figure 1).

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Skills per category, split by whether the skill ships files under scripts/. Every such skill has a corresponding test-suite directory. The existence of a suite does not establish that every helper or code path is exercised; a documentation-only skill leaves implementation to the agent.
figures.headline: Of 163 skills, 154 ship reference documents and 105 ship executable scripts, with counts varying across the 16 categories.
citing_sentences: Of these, 105 ship executable code under scripts/ and 154 ship reference documents (Figure 2).
For reporting, we assigned each of the 163 skills exactly one primary category by its dominant intent; these assignments yield the 16 categories in Table C.1 and Figure 2.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: The 78 databases documented by the database-lookup skill at tag v2.65.0. (A) Databases by domain, using the skill’s own grouping, which we checked against the reference files on disk. (B) Access constraints from the skill’s own tables: 57 databases document no credential requirement, 18 require a free-registration key, and 3 are paid or otherwise restricted; each restricted database has a named free alternative.
figures.headline: Of 78 databases, 57 need no credential and 18 require a key, and the 3 restricted ones each have a free alternative.
citing_sentences: Data retrieval skills handle identifier resolution and query construction against named resources; one skill, database-lookup, alone documents 78 databases across 9 domains, of which 57 document no credential requirement and 18 require a key (Figure 3).
Its 80 files include 2 cross-cutting guides, and its coverage is concentrated in biology and genomics (Figure 3).

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: How the 46 documented workflows compose skills at tag v2.65.0. The 44 skills named by at least 3 workflows are arranged by domain group, with the number of workflows naming each skill after its name. A chord joins each of the 147 pairs that at least 3 workflows name together, and its width grows with that count. The six groups colour our 16-category taxonomy and are used only here. The figure describes our own worked examples, not observed agent sessions.
figures.headline: Documented workflows combine skills unevenly, with 44 skills named by at least 3 workflows and 147 pairs recurring together.
citing_sentences: Each of the 46 worked examples in docs/examples.md names the skills it draws on, and the median example spans 4 of the 16 categories (Figure 4).

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Lexical separability of the always-resident descriptions at tag v2.65.0. (A) Each skill’s cosine to its nearest neighbour; most descriptions have no lexically close competitor. (B) The ten closest pairs, marked by whether either description points to the other. (C) The share of the $k$ most similar pairs carrying such a pointer. Cosine is a lexical proxy for confusability, not a measurement of any host’s selection behaviour.
figures.headline: Most descriptions lack a close lexical neighbour, and explicit pointers cover 17 of the twenty closest pairs.
citing_sentences: The median skill’s nearest neighbour has a cosine similarity of 0.15, and the ninetieth percentile is 0.26 (Figure 5A), so a typical skill has no lexically close competitor.

The next most similar pairs also connect adjacent work in the same domain: two cheminformatics toolkits, two study-design skills, two quantum-computing frameworks and two plotting libraries (Figure 5B).
Pointers cover 17 of the twenty closest pairs, 26 of the fifty closest, and 33 of the hundred closest (Figure 5C).

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: Token costs for the library’s 46 documented workflows at tag v2.65.0, compared with a 200,000-token reference window. (A) Cost with the resident tier and instruction files, and after adding every reference file of every named skill; the shaded gap is the deferred tier. The upper series is an upper bound by construction. (B) The share of its own reference material each workflow could load before exhausting the window. Both panels count documentation text only, excluding scripts, assets, tool output and host wrappers.
figures.headline: Instruction files fit the 200,000-token window for all 46 workflows, but loading every reference file exceeds it for 29.
citing_sentences: 0 of the 46 workflows exceed the window (Figure 6A).
The median documented workflow can afford 85% of its own reference material, the lower quartile can afford 61%, and the most demanding workflow can afford 35% (Figure 6B).

abstract: A language-model agent asked to analyse an experiment will usually return working code. Whether the analysis is defensible is a different question. A defensible analysis depends on procedural choices: which test the field accepts, which identifier namespace is authoritative, and which caveats must accompany a result. We present Scientific Agent Skills, an open library of 163 such procedures in 16 areas of practice, including genomics, cheminformatics, medical imaging, study design and scientific communication. Each skill is a directory built around a versioned, human-readable instruction file. An agent loads the file only when a task calls for it; the directory often also contains reference material and runnable scripts. We report no task-level evaluation and no host selection rate. We measure two properties of the documentation corpus: the always-resident descriptions of all 163 skills cost 7.1% of a 200,000-token window, and the median documented workflow fits within 23.9% of it, although 29 of 46 would overflow if every reference file were loaded. Openly licensed and available at https://github.com/K-Dense-AI/scientific-agent-skills.

sections.body: The introduction gives examples of procedural errors an agent can make, such as omitting multiple-testing correction or counting cells as independent replicates. It defines an agent skill as a directory with an instruction file that a host loads only when a task calls for it. The paper introduces Scientific Agent Skills, a library of 163 skills, and states that it reports no task-level evaluation. Sections 4 and 5 measure description separation and the context cost of documented workflows. The authors wrote most of the skills, so the paper describes their own artifact rather than an independent audit. It is a resource paper and does not validate any individual skill.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Agents often return working code that is not defensible, so the paper proposes a library of field-specific procedures packaged as agent skills.

sections.body: A skill is a directory containing an instruction file with a short header limited to six fields. The design uses three disclosure tiers: the name and description of every skill stay resident, the instruction body is read when the agent judges the skill relevant, and reference documents are read only when the instruction body points to them. At tag v2.65.0 the resident tier is 14,246 tokens, a median of 67 tokens per skill, compared with 482,506 tokens of complete instruction files. Holding the whole library in context costs 7.1% of a 200,000-token window. The authors state that tiering defers cost rather than removing it, and that routing relies on the resident tier alone.
sections.heading: What an agent skill is
sections.headline: Each skill is a directory whose instruction file is read only when relevant, keeping most documentation out of standing context.

sections.body: This section describes how the library is organised and identifies four recurring skill types: package workflows, data retrieval, research platforms and method skills. The 16 categories are the authors' reporting convention rather than a property of the repository. Scientific communication and figures is the largest category in Table C.1. The database-lookup skill alone documents 78 databases, of which 57 document no credential requirement and 18 require a key. Each of the 46 worked examples names the skills it draws on, and the median example spans 4 of the 16 categories. Of the 162 skills named, 81 appear in exactly one example, whereas scientific-visualization appears in 27 examples.
sections.heading: What the library covers
sections.headline: The library's 163 skills cover 16 self-assigned categories, most shipping reference documents, and the workflows combine them unevenly.

sections.body: This section measures cosine similarity between bag-of-words descriptions as a lexical proxy for confusability, not as a measure of any host's selection behaviour. The median skill's nearest neighbour has a cosine of 0.15, and the ninetieth percentile is 0.26. The closest pair, datamol and rdkit, reaches 0.40. The authors added 56 pointers connecting 44 distinct pairs, and pointers cover 17 of the twenty closest pairs. Infographics and scientific-schematics, at 0.36, is the closest unguarded pair. The third-party security scanner flags 301 pairs but catches 0 of the twenty closest. The authors note that no host reports a selection rate, so this measure does not estimate an error rate.
sections.heading: Can descriptions distinguish among skills?
sections.headline: Most skill descriptions are lexically well separated, but a few neighbouring pairs remain close and some lack authored guidance.

sections.body: The authors costed the 46 worked examples, treating each as a session. After the resident tier and instruction files are included, the median workflow costs 47,706 tokens, or 23.9% of the window, and none exceeds it. Loading every reference file of every named skill raises the median to 225,498 tokens, or 112.7%, and 29 of the 46 workflows then exceed the window. The median workflow can afford 85% of its own reference material within the remaining budget. These figures count documentation text only, excluding scripts, assets and host wrappers, so they understate session context. The authors recommend installing only the skills a project needs, but state that whether this improves selection is untested.
sections.heading: Do the skills a workflow needs fit in context?
sections.headline: Documented workflows fit a 200,000-token window in their instruction files, but 29 of 46 overflow if every reference file loads.

sections.body: This section lists the limits of the study. The paper contains no controlled comparison of agent outcomes with and without skills, so it does not show that skills improve scientific work. Selection is measured by lexical similarity of descriptions, not by how often a host selects the correct skill. A selected skill can still fail if the agent omits steps or if the study violates the procedure's assumptions. The installed-base estimate in Appendix H counts cloning clients, not scientists or sessions. Host portability is described as intended but untested. Of the 163 skills, 32 do not list the authors as author, and 4 name no author. The structural contract covers 105 skills and leaves 2 broken local paths outside its gate.
sections.heading: Limitations
sections.headline: The paper reports no task-level evaluation, measures selection only as a lexical proxy, and does not test host portability.

sections.body: The library is available on GitHub under an open licence at tag v2.65.0, released 2026-08-29, at commit f6fcafeb1cc8c82eca0160a18bc41c38427b8e0f. The repository documentation names six hosts as supported, a claim Section 6 qualifies. The repository had 37,905 GitHub stars at the time of writing. No analysis package is released, but every corpus-derived quantity is computed from the public tree with NumPy and Matplotlib. The authors say a citation without a tag does not identify what was run. A paper reporting a result from a specific skill should name that skill and its `metadata.version`, and clinical, regulatory or imaging skills should state their scope limits.
sections.heading: Availability and citation
sections.headline: Work using the library should cite the paper and tag v2.65.0, and name each skill's metadata version.

sections.body: Appendix A defines the tokenizer as `o200k_base`, which counts raw file text, and the documentation corpus of 2,963,180 tokens. It gives the token ledger, including that at most 89 skills fit in the window when the shortest are installed first. Appendix B reports that 154 skills ship reference documents and 105 ship executable scripts under scripts/. Appendix C gives the category counts. Appendix G varies the routing preprocessing, and at least 9 of the original 10 closest pairs remain in each alternative's top 10. Appendix H estimates the installed base from a 14-day traffic window, and the authors state that this estimate is not evidence of benefit.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendices list the tokenizer and token ledger, skill contents, category counts, routing sensitivity and installed-base estimate.
